[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#purpose-statement]

### Purpose Statement

This guidance defines the three practitioner tiers of the SDLC AI Consumer-Centric Self-Service model — High-Tech, Mid-Tech, and Low-Tech — and establishes which tier can build which AI and automation capability type, under what conditions, and with what governance accountability. It provides the role assignment and escalation framework for the enterprise AI governance model.
page_texts.5:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#business-value]

### Business Value

The role model prevents two failure modes: the gatekeeper anti-pattern (requiring High-Tech involvement for every AI capability build) and the unscoped build anti-pattern (Low-Tech practitioners building capabilities beyond their tier's skill and governance profile). It establishes clear accountability for quality gate reviews without creating a central bottleneck.
page_texts.6:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#target-audience]

### Target Audience

- **Primary Audience**: Enterprise architects, platform governance team, and domain product owners assigning build ownership
- **Secondary Audience**: All practitioners proposing or building AI and automation capabilities
- **Stakeholders**: Role Champions and COE Accelerators in each functional community
page_texts.8:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#applicable-scenarios]

#### Applicable Scenarios

- Onboarding a team or individual to the SDLC AI platform
- Determining which AI tools, content areas, and collaboration channels are appropriate for a given role
- Assigning Role Champions or COE Accelerators within a business unit
- Evaluating whether the correct build tier is assigned to a proposed capability during intake review
- Governing a capability promotion from Pilot to Production — ensuring the correct governance sign-off tier is engaged
page_texts.9:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#scope-boundaries]

#### Scope Boundaries

- **In Scope**: Role tier definitions, build capability scope, governance accountability, collaboration model, escalation indicators
- **Out of Scope**: Platform permissions and access controls — this guidance describes role expectations and engagement patterns, not system entitlements
- **Related Guidance**: [GUID-TEC-AI-001: AI and Automation Classification Guidance](../../technology/ai/GUID-TEC-AI-001-ai-automation-classification-guidance.md) must be applied first to classify the capability before build tier assignment

page_texts.12:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#business-drivers]

#### Business Drivers

- SDLC AI platforms enable practitioners at all technical levels to build AI capabilities; without role-based build boundaries, governance accountability is unclear
- High-Tech practitioners are a limited resource; routing all AI capability builds through them creates bottlenecks that contradict the self-service model
- Each practitioner tier has genuine and distinct AI capability needs; a single build path does not serve all tiers equally
page_texts.13:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#strategic-alignment]

#### Strategic Alignment

This guidance implements the SDLC AI Consumer-Centric Self-Service model and is the organizational design layer of the enterprise AI governance framework (ADR-GOV-011). Two governing principles apply to all tiers: Drive to Self-Service and Crowd Source and Collaborate.
page_texts.15:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#current-state-assessment]

#### Current State Assessment

- AI agent platform capabilities (M365 Copilot Agent Builder, Copilot Studio) are accessible to all practitioner tiers, including Low-Tech practitioners who are not expected to build software
- Without defined build boundaries, any practitioner can build and publish any type of AI capability, including Custom AI Agents that require engineering-level governance
page_texts.17:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#problem-description]

#### Problem Description

In the absence of explicit role-based build boundaries, organizations experience two failure patterns: centralization (all builds routed to High-Tech, creating a bottleneck and contradicting self-service) and unbounded building (Low-Tech practitioners configuring capabilities that exceed their governance capacity, creating compliance risk). A role model that maps build capability to tier prevents both.

page_texts.20:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#principle-1-drive-to-self-service]

#### Principle 1: Drive to Self-Service

**Description:** Every tier is expected to consume AI capabilities independently, not through intermediaries. Tooling, content, and agents are designed to be accessible without requiring expert facilitation.

**Rationale:** Self-service is the only model that scales to the volume of AI capability consumption that modern delivery requires. Intermediary-mediated consumption creates bottlenecks and reduces the organization's ability to extract value from AI investments.

**Application:** Design onboarding, templates, and intake processes to minimize friction for the lowest applicable tier. Route facilitation requests back to self-service resources rather than providing human assistance for tasks the tier can complete independently.
page_texts.21:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#principle-2-crowd-source-and-collaborate]

#### Principle 2: Crowd Source and Collaborate

**Description:** Each tier is expected to contribute back to the ecosystem through shared prompts, templates, discussions, and standards. Individual expertise at all levels strengthens the collective capability of the organization.

**Rationale:** The organization's collective AI capability compounds when every practitioner shares what works. A model of silent consumption reduces the return on AI platform investment.

**Application:** Include contribution expectations explicitly in role definitions. Role Champions and COE Accelerators are responsible for creating contribution opportunities and recognizing contributors within their tier.
page_texts.23:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#approach-1-the-three-tier-role-model]

#### Approach 1: The Three-Tier Role Model

**Overview:** Three practitioner tiers define build capability and governance accountability.

| Dimension | High-Tech (Arch, Dev, Infra) | Mid-Tech (QA, Config) | Low-Tech (PM, SM, BA) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Engagement mode | Publish and Collaborate | Publish | Collaborate |
| Primary content areas | Architecture Strategy; Software Utils and Frameworks | Frameworks; How-To Guides | Enterprise Home; Community Collaboration; AI Policy |
| Authoring expectation | Standards, agents, frameworks | Process guides, templates | Golden prompts, how-to contributions |
| AI tooling fluency | Code-level and conversational | Functional and conversational | Conversational |
| COE role focus | Build and validate reusable technical components | Scale delivery-domain AI practices | Drive adoption and surface practitioner needs |
page_texts.24:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#approach-2-the-build-capability-matrix]

#### Approach 2: The Build Capability Matrix

**Overview:** Maps each capability type to the build tier that can own it.

| Capability Type | Low-Tech (PM, SM, BA) | Mid-Tech (QA, Config) | High-Tech (Arch, Dev, Infra) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automation — Workflow (no-code) | Build with oversight | Build independently | Build independently |
| Automation — RPA and Workflow (complex) | Out of scope | Build independently | Build independently |
| Intelligent Automation | Out of scope | Build with High-Tech support | Build independently |
| AI Agents (Configured) | Build with oversight | Build independently | Standards and patterns; not primary authors |
| Custom AI Agents | Out of scope | Out of scope | Build independently |

**Legend:**
- **Build independently:** Role has the skill and knowledge to complete the build without tier escalation
- **Build with oversight:** Role can perform the configuration work but requires review from a higher tier before the capability is promoted to Pilot, enters Production, or is shared
- **Build with High-Tech support:** Role leads the process design but must collaborate with a High-Tech role for AI model configuration, validation, or integration
- **Out of scope:** The required skill profile is not part of this tier's expected capability; build requests should be escalated or routed to the appropriate tier
page_texts.26:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#best-practice-1-high-tech-roles-define-standards-not-individual-agents]

#### Best Practice 1: High-Tech Roles Define Standards, Not Individual Agents

**Description:** High-Tech roles are responsible for standards, frameworks, quality gates, and governance review — not for authoring individual configured agents for Low-Tech or Mid-Tech use cases.

**Rationale:** High-Tech roles that author individual PM, SM, or BA agents at scale become a bottleneck and contradict the self-service principle. Their value is in enabling other tiers to build correctly, not in building on their behalf.

**Implementation:** High-Tech role COE responsibilities explicitly include building and validating reusable agent frameworks and prompt patterns, and owning quality-gate review — not individual agent authoring for other tiers.

**Success Indicators:** High-Tech practitioners are not the primary authors of team-scoped configured agents; they are the quality gate reviewers.
page_texts.27:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#best-practice-2-all-agents-require-high-tech-governance-review-before-production]

#### Best Practice 2: All Agents Require High-Tech Governance Review Before Production

**Description:** Regardless of which tier built a capability, High-Tech sign-off is required before any configured or custom AI agent reaches Production state.

**Rationale:** Build ownership and governance sign-off are separate responsibilities. A Mid-Tech or Low-Tech builder has domain expertise in the capability's content; a High-Tech reviewer has the AI governance expertise to assess quality gate compliance.

**Implementation:** The Pilot-to-Production quality gate requires explicit High-Tech sign-off as documented in STD-TEC-AI-001 and STD-TEC-AI-005.

**Success Indicators:** No configured or custom AI agent reaches Production state without a recorded High-Tech governance review.
page_texts.29:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#pitfall-1-treating-tiers-as-a-seniority-hierarchy]

#### Pitfall 1: Treating Tiers as a Seniority Hierarchy

**Description:** Treating this model as a seniority or value hierarchy rather than a capability and engagement model.

**Impact:** Undermines cross-tier collaboration and contribution; Low-Tech practitioners disengage if they feel their contributions are devalued.

**Prevention:** Frame tier definitions explicitly as capability and engagement models, not levels of organizational importance.

**Mitigation:** Role Champion responsibilities (all tiers) include recognizing contributors within their tier, reinforcing that contribution at every tier has organizational value.
page_texts.30:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#pitfall-2-gatekeeper-model]

#### Pitfall 2: Gatekeeper Model

**Description:** Requiring Low-Tech or Mid-Tech roles to route all AI requests through High-Tech intermediaries.

**Impact:** Contradicts the self-service principle; creates bottlenecks; reduces the value of AI platform investment.

**Prevention:** The collaboration model defines specifically where High-Tech input is required — at defined governance gates, not as a prerequisite for every build.

**Mitigation:** If High-Tech practitioners are consistently receiving requests that belong to Mid-Tech or Low-Tech self-service, the intake process or onboarding for those tiers needs improvement.
page_texts.31:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#pitfall-3-champion-without-community]

#### Pitfall 3: Champion Without Community

**Description:** Assigning Role Champions or COE Accelerators without giving them dedicated time, channels, and recognition mechanisms.

**Impact:** Makes the role nominal rather than functional; does not produce the contribution and adoption outcomes the model requires.

**Prevention:** Role Champion designation must include formal time allocation, community channel access, and recognition participation.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#preparation-steps]

#### Preparation Steps

1. **Assign builds to the correct tier during intake review**

    - Required inputs: the build capability matrix; the capability's taxonomy classification (from GUID-TEC-AI-001)
    - Key activity: match the capability type to the build tier column and confirm the proposer's tier
    - Expected output: recorded build tier assignment in the capability registry

2. **Identify escalation indicators before build begins**

    - Required inputs: the escalation indicators section of this guidance
    - Key activity: review whether any escalation condition applies to the proposed capability
    - Expected output: escalation decision documented in the intake record
page_texts.38:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#execution-steps]

#### Execution Steps

1. **Apply the collaboration model for cross-tier builds**

    | Scenario | Lead Role | Supporting Role | Handoff Point |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | Low-Tech builds a configured agent for team use | Low-Tech | High-Tech (governance review) | Agent moves from Pilot to Production |
    | Low-Tech builds a workflow that connects to a shared system | Low-Tech (process design) | Mid-Tech or High-Tech (integration review) | Before workflow is shared or scaled |
    | Mid-Tech builds Intelligent Automation with an AI model step | Mid-Tech (process design) | High-Tech (model configuration and review) | Model configuration and monitoring setup |
    | Mid-Tech builds a configured agent that connects to production systems | Mid-Tech | High-Tech (integration architecture review) | Integration configuration |
    | High-Tech builds a Custom AI Agent for a Low-Tech use case | High-Tech | Low-Tech (requirements, output validation) | Requirements definition; output acceptance testing |
    | Any tier builds an agent reaching Production state | Builder tier | High-Tech (governance quality gate) | Promotion from Pilot to Production |
page_texts.40:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#decision-point-1-which-tier-should-build-this-capability]

#### Decision Point 1: Which Tier Should Build This Capability?

**Context:** During intake review, when a capability proposal has been classified and a build owner needs to be assigned.

**Options:** Low-Tech, Mid-Tech, High-Tech, or cross-tier with defined collaboration

**Criteria:** Apply the build capability matrix — match the capability type to the column for the proposer's tier; if "Out of scope," route to the appropriate tier

**Recommendation:** Use the matrix as the primary routing tool. Cross-tier collaboration scenarios are defined explicitly; if a scenario does not match a matrix row, escalate to the Platform Governance Team.
page_texts.41:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#decision-point-2-does-this-build-require-escalation-before-starting]

#### Decision Point 2: Does This Build Require Escalation Before Starting?

**Context:** Any tier evaluating whether their proposed capability is within scope.

**Options:** Proceed within tier, escalate to higher tier, or route to cross-tier collaboration

**Criteria:** Escalation indicators (see below)

**Recommendation:**

For Low-Tech roles, escalate when:
- The capability requires connecting to a data source or system the builder does not personally have access to
- The workflow involves more than one system and requires API or connector configuration
- The agent is expected to take actions (create, update, delete) in systems rather than only retrieve and summarize
- The capability is intended for use by more than one team or will be published to a shared space

For Mid-Tech roles, escalate when:
- The Intelligent Automation build requires training or fine-tuning an AI model rather than using a pre-built platform service
- The automation or agent connects to a system requiring architecture-level access
- The build requires custom code to extend platform capabilities

For any tier, escalate when:
- The capability is intended for an external-facing channel — external-facing deployment is outside the scope of this framework; a separate enterprise approval process governs external-facing AI capabilities
- The capability handles regulated data (PII, financial, legal, compliance-relevant)
- The capability must meet SLA requirements that exceed what the build tier can operationally support

page_texts.43:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#example-1-low-tech-pm-building-a-configured-agent]

### Example 1: Low-Tech (PM) Building a Configured Agent

A Program Manager (Low-Tech) identifies a need for a daily briefing agent that aggregates meeting summaries and open action items. The PM classifies the capability using GUID-TEC-AI-001 as an AI Agent (Configured). Per the build capability matrix, Low-Tech can build configured agents with oversight. The PM uses the golden path intake form (PTN-GOV-AI-010), completes the capability contract and output contract templates with input from a Role Champion, and submits the agent for High-Tech governance review before requesting Pilot promotion. The PM builds independently but the High-Tech sign-off gate is not bypassed.
page_texts.44:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#example-2-mid-tech-qa-engineer-building-intelligent-automation]

### Example 2: Mid-Tech (QA Engineer) Building Intelligent Automation

A QA Engineer (Mid-Tech) wants to build an Intelligent Automation capability that routes defect reports to the correct team based on content analysis. The capability requires connecting to the defect tracking system. Per the build capability matrix, Mid-Tech can build Intelligent Automation with High-Tech support for the model configuration step. The QA Engineer leads the process design and evidence map definition; a High-Tech architect configures the AI model classification step and validates the integration architecture. Both roles sign off before Pilot promotion.
page_texts.45:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#example-3-high-tech-architect-building-a-custom-ai-agent]

### Example 3: High-Tech Architect Building a Custom AI Agent

A High-Tech architect builds a Custom AI Agent that synthesizes architecture decisions and produces impact assessments for proposed changes. The architect uses the contract-first pattern (PTN-TEC-AI-009), authors all four contract artifacts, and produces a System Connection Register for the connections to the decision records repository and capability registry. A separate High-Tech reviewer who was not involved in the build performs the governance quality gate review, preserving the independent check required by this role model. The capability is registered in the portfolio registry and undergoes standard lifecycle quality gates.

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#governance-structure]

#### Governance Structure

- The Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board owns the role model and approves any changes to tier definitions or build capability scope
- The Platform Governance Team applies the model during intake review and enforces tier assignment
- High-Tech roles own quality-gate review for all configured and custom AI agent promotions to Production
- Role Champions within each tier are responsible for adoption and contribution within their functional communities
page_texts.50:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#organizational-compliance]

#### Organizational Compliance

- All capabilities handling regulated data must follow the escalation indicators that apply regardless of tier (external-facing channels, regulated data, SLA requirements)
- Governance accountability is recorded in the capability contract per STD-TEC-AI-001

[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#success-criteria]

### Success Criteria

The role model is operating effectively when the following measurable outcomes are achieved:

| Metric | Target | Measurement Method |
|---|---|---|
| % of agents in Pilot or Production with recorded build tier assignment | 100% | Capability registry audit at governance gate |
| % of agents promoted to Production with a recorded High-Tech governance review | 100% | Lifecycle quality gate records |
| % of Low-Tech-built agents that received oversight review before Pilot promotion | 100% | Governance gate records |
| % of Mid-Tech Intelligent Automation builds with documented High-Tech collaboration at model configuration step | 100% | Change records and capability contracts |
| Role Champion coverage across functional communities | At least one designated Role Champion per major delivery domain | Role Champion registry |
| Time to onboard a new practitioner to the correct tier | Declining over time as Role Champions become active | Onboarding records |
page_texts.56:
[strategy/guidance/governance/processes/GUID-GOV-PROC-009-sdlc-ai-consumer-role-model.md#assessment-cadence]

### Assessment Cadence

- **Quarterly tier review**: The Platform Governance Team reviews role tier assignments and escalation patterns for the prior quarter. Findings are used to refine the build capability matrix and update escalation indicator guidance.
- **Annual model review**: The Enterprise Copilot Architecture Board reviews the role model for structural changes — new tier definitions, capability type additions, or changes to governance accountability — based on quarterly review findings and portfolio evolution.
